title: Blessings on the Level Ground
sum: Two Sabbath disputes open the chapter. When his disciples rub heads of grain on the Sabbath, Jesus points to David and claims that the Son of Man is Lord over the Sabbath. On another Sabbath he heals a man's withered right hand in a synagogue, asking whether the day is for doing good or harm, saving life or destroying it, and his critics are filled with fury. After a night of prayer on the mountain, he chooses twelve of his disciples and names them apostles.

Then he comes down to a level place crowded with disciples and people from Judea, Jerusalem and the Phoenician coast, and gives Luke's great sermon, the Sermon on the Plain. Four blessings on the poor, hungry, weeping and hated are matched by four woes on the rich, full, laughing and admired. The heart of it is love for enemies: bless, pray, give, lend without hope of return, and be compassionate as the Father is. It ends with warnings about judging, blind guides, trees and their fruit, and two builders, one who hears and acts and one who only hears.
readings: Read as ethics for a new community

Many read the sermon as Jesus' charter for his followers: a community that reverses the world's values, shares its goods, and meets hostility with love. Luke's version, with its blessings on the materially poor and its woes on the rich, is the basis of much Christian social teaching, from the church fathers' sermons on almsgiving to Catholic social teaching and liberation theology.

Others stress that the blessings are not first of all commands but announcements: God's reign is arriving, and with it the reversal of present conditions. The "now" and the "then" in 6:21 and 6:25 place the hearers between the present age and the coming one, as Mary's song did (1:51–53).

Read beside the Sermon on the Mount, Luke's sermon is shorter (30 verses against 107), sharper about money, and silent on the Law of Moses, which fills Matthew 5:17–48. Most scholars think both draw on a common source of sayings (Q) and that each shaped it for his readers: Matthew for Jewish believers concerned with righteousness and the Law, Luke for Gentile readers in mixed communities of rich and poor.

views.H: Galilee's economy explains much: small farmers burdened with taxes and debt, day laborers, and a thin layer of the rich around Herod Antipas' court. Lending, robbery of cloaks and grain measures were everyday matters. The Sabbath disputes reflect real debates among Jewish teachers over which acts counted as work; the Mishnah later lists thirty-nine categories. The Twelve include Matthew (Matthew 9:9 identifies him with the tax collector whom Luke calls Levi in Luke 5:27) and a man called the Zealot, two ends of Galilee's politics.
views.C: Luke follows Mark 2:23–3:19 for the Sabbath stories and the Twelve, but reverses Mark's order of the crowds and the choosing, so the Twelve come down with Jesus to hear the sermon. The sermon itself is from the double tradition shared with Matthew, often called Q; Luke's form is widely thought closer to Q's order and length, while Matthew's "poor in spirit" and "hunger for righteousness" may be his own expansions. Some (the Farrer-Goulder view) think Luke instead shortened Matthew.
views.L: Luke builds a deliberate ascent and descent: up the mountain to pray and choose (6:12–16), down to the plain to heal and teach (6:17–19). The sermon has a clear shape: blessings and woes (6:20–26), love of enemies framed by "keep loving your enemies" (6:27, 35), judging and giving (6:37–42), and the tests of fruit and obedience (6:43–49). The reversal theme of Mary's song (1:51–53) here becomes Jesus' own teaching.
views.J: The Sabbath stories are debates inside Judaism, not attacks on it: whether rubbing grain was threshing, whether healing a non-urgent illness could wait. Jewish law agreed that saving life overrode the Sabbath. Love of enemies extends Leviticus 19:18 and Exodus 23:4–5; the Golden Rule had a negative form in Tobit and Hillel; "compassionate, the way your Father is" echoes a common Jewish teaching about imitating God. Amy-Jill Levine warns readers not to sharpen Jesus' sayings by caricaturing the Judaism around him.
views.T: Luke's sayings on poverty fed the monastic ideal of voluntary poverty, from the desert fathers to Francis of Assisi; the sermon also shaped the church's long ban on lending at interest, and modern Catholic teaching on the preferential option for the poor. Luke 6:36, "Become compassionate," was chosen as the motto of the Catholic Jubilee of Mercy (2015–2016). The list of the Twelve gave the church its calendar of apostles' feasts.

deep.h: The Sermon on the Plain and the Sermon on the Mount
deep.b:
Luke's sermon (6:20–49) and Matthew's (Matthew 5–7) begin with blessings and end with two builders, and in between share love of enemies, the Golden Rule, judging, the speck and the beam, and trees and fruit, in nearly the same order. Matthew has much more: the Law and the antitheses (Matthew 5:17–48), giving, prayer and fasting in secret, the Lord's Prayer, treasure, worry. Many of those sayings appear elsewhere in Luke (11:2–4; 12:22–34; 16:17–18).

Most scholars explain this by a shared sayings source, Q, which Luke kept closer to its original form and order and Matthew enlarged with other teaching (Two-Source view). Others think Luke knew Matthew's sermon and cut it down (Farrer-Goulder view), moving the rest to fit his travel narrative. Traditional harmonies held that Jesus taught similar things on more than one occasion, and that Luke's "level place" may have been on the mountainside (two sermons or one occasion). On every view, the two sermons share a center: love that goes beyond what is owed, and obedience that goes beyond hearing.

Luke's four blessings and four woes stand in pairs: poor and rich, hungry and full, weeping and laughing, hated and praised. The form is old. Deuteronomy's blessings and curses (Deuteronomy 28), the prophets' woes (Isaiah 5:8–23), and the Epistle of Enoch's woes on the rich (1 Enoch 94–105) all set choices and outcomes side by side. Jesus speaks them as announcements: God's reign is turning things over.

Readers have asked whether poverty itself is blessed and wealth itself cursed. The church fathers mostly answered that the poor are blessed because God is on their side and they have nothing to hold them back, and that the rich are warned not for having goods but for trusting them and ignoring the poor (16:19–31). Liberation theologians read the blessing as God's partiality for the oppressed. Others read Luke's poor as the faithful humble of Israel, close to Matthew's "poor in spirit." Luke's own book keeps both: real poverty matters (14:13; 16:20), and the rich can be saved by generosity (19:8–9).

deep.title: Claude's theory: a sermon for patrons
deep.b: This is Claude's suggestion. Luke's sermon spends unusual time on lending, giving and "thanks" (charis, 6:32–35). In the Greek and Roman world, gifts and loans created ties of patronage: the giver expected honor and favors in return. Luke's first readers likely included people of means, such as Theophilus, "most excellent" (1:3), and patrons like the women of 8:3 and the centurion of 7:5. The sermon may be aimed at them in particular, telling patrons in the church to give without building networks of obligation, as God gives to the ungrateful. Scholars of Luke's social world (Halvor Moxnes, Joel Green and others) have discussed patronage in Luke; reading the sermon's middle section as a word to patrons is a narrower claim of Claude's.

echoes: Deuteronomy 23:25; Exodus 34:21; 1 Samuel 21:1–6; Leviticus 24:5–9; Mark 2:23–3:19; Matthew 12:1–14; Matthew 10:1–4; Matthew 5:1–7:29; Isaiah 61:1–3; 1 Samuel 2:5–8; 1:51–53; Leviticus 19:18; Exodus 23:4–5; Tobit 4:15; 1 Enoch 94:8; Proverbs 10:25; Ezekiel 13:10–14; Acts 1:13; Acts 1:21–26; James 2:5; James 5:1–6

settings.what: The grain fields on the Sabbath
settings.to: Jesus' disciples, challenged by some Pharisees in the fields of Galilee
settings.when: On a Sabbath, as the disciples pick and rub heads of grain while walking
settings.why: The Pharisees press a real question of Sabbath law: whether rubbing grain counts as harvest work forbidden on God's day. Jesus answers from Scripture, with David's need overriding the rule about holy bread, and then with a claim about himself: the Son of Man has authority over how the Sabbath is kept. The law at stake is the Torah's command to rest (Exodus 20:8–11; 34:21) as Pharisaic teachers applied it; it bound every Jew.
settings.readers: For Luke's largely Gentile readers, who did not keep the Sabbath, the story shows that Jesus kept the Sabbath while claiming authority over it, and that his followers' freedom came from him, not from contempt for Israel's Law.
views: Many scholars (Sanders, Vermes) see a typical dispute between Jewish teachers over how strictly to apply the Sabbath.
Others stress that Luke ends with "the Son of Man is Lord over the Sabbath" without Mark's humane reason, making the scene about Jesus' authority.

settings.what: Healing a withered hand on the Sabbath
settings.to: The synagogue congregation, with scribes and Pharisees watching closely
settings.when: On another Sabbath, while Jesus is teaching in a synagogue
settings.why: Knowing his critics' thoughts, Jesus brings the man into the middle and asks the question openly: is the Sabbath for doing good or harm, for saving life or destroying it? He refuses to treat an act of healing as neutral work that could wait. The question binds his hearers to decide what God's day is for.
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw that Jesus' opponents were angry rather than convinced, and that the conflict which will lead to Jerusalem was already growing.

settings.to: His disciples, whom he looks at directly (6:20), with the Twelve just chosen, and a great crowd from Judea, Jerusalem and the coast of Tyre and Sidon listening (6:17; 7:1)
settings.when: On level ground at the foot of the mountain, after a night of prayer and the choosing of the Twelve, while he is healing the sick. Matthew sets the sermon on a mountain, with Jesus seated and the disciples coming to him (Matthew 5:1–2; 7:28–29); Luke sets it on level ground among the crowds and the sick.
settings.why: To announce God's reversal to people who are poor, hungry and hated for his sake, to warn the comfortable, and to describe the way of life of his followers: love of enemies, giving without return, mercy as the Father's mercy, honest self-judgment, and obedience that acts on what it hears. Spoken to disciples within the crowd's hearing, it is both instruction for the committed and an invitation to the rest.
settings.readers: Luke's readers were mixed communities of rich and poor, Jews and Gentiles, some of them facing suspicion or exclusion. The sermon told them how to live as a community where patrons give without expecting returns and where enemies are loved.
views: Most read 6:20 as addressing disciples, so the blessings describe those who have already left things to follow Jesus (5:11, 28).
Others stress 7:1, "in the people's hearing," and see the sermon as public preaching to all Israel.

settings.to: The disciples in front of him; the woes speak to "you who are rich," whether present or not
settings.when: The opening of the sermon
settings.why: To declare God's favor on those who have nothing now and God's warning to those who have everything now. The woes call the rich to see their danger before it is too late, as the prophets' woes did.
settings.readers: Luke's richer readers heard a warning and a call to share; poorer readers heard that God was on their side.

settings.to: "You who are listening" (6:27): every hearer willing to take it in
settings.when: The center of the sermon. Matthew places love of enemies inside the six contrasts with what was said in the Law (Matthew 5:38–48); Luke has no Law frame.
settings.why: To set a standard beyond the give-and-take of ordinary society: bless those who curse, give to those who take, lend without expecting return, because that is how God treats the ungrateful. It forms a community recognizable by mercy.
settings.readers: For Christians facing insult and loss, and for those with goods to lend, the words defined what made them different from "sinners."

settings.what: The parable of the blind guide and the splinter and beam
settings.to: The disciples, especially those who will teach others
settings.when: After the call not to judge
settings.why: To warn would-be teachers that they cannot lead others where they cannot see, and that self-examination must come before correcting a brother. Matthew uses the blind-guide saying against the Pharisees (Matthew 15:14); Luke turns it on the disciples themselves.
settings.readers: Leaders in Luke's churches heard a warning against hypocrisy in their own ranks.

settings.what: Trees and fruit; the two builders
settings.to: All who call him "Lord" and hear his words
settings.when: The close of the sermon. Matthew uses the tree saying twice, against false prophets (Matthew 7:15–20) and against the Pharisees (Matthew 12:33–35), and his builders are tested by rain, floods and wind (Matthew 7:24–27); Luke's by a river in flood.
settings.why: To make action the test of a hearer: a good tree shows itself in fruit, and a house shows its foundation in a flood. The final picture urges hearers to build their lives on doing what he says before the storm comes.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, already calling Jesus "Lord," were warned that confession without obedience will not stand.

traditions.q: Does "Blessed are the poor" give the materially poor a special place in God's eyes?
views: Yes, in a qualified sense: the Church teaches a "preferential love" or option for the poor, drawn from texts like Luke 6:20 (Catechism 2443–2448; the Latin American bishops at Puebla, 1979). It also warned against reading this through Marxist class struggle (Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Libertatis Nuntius, 1984).

The fathers read Luke's poor as truly poor and urged the rich to share: John Chrysostom preached that not sharing one's goods with the poor is theft from them, and Basil said the bread you store belongs to the hungry. Voluntary poverty is honored in monastic life, but poverty is not a merit in itself.

Luther read Luke's blessing together with Matthew's "poor in spirit": it is not outward poverty that makes a person blessed but a heart that does not trust in riches. He attacked monastic vows of poverty as a false way of earning merit, while urging generosity to the needy.

Many Anabaptists read the sermon as a direct rule for the community: the Hutterites practiced full community of goods, and Mennonite communities stress mutual aid and simple living as obedience to Jesus' teaching on wealth.

Most evangelicals read the poor of Luke 6:20 as both the economically poor and the humble who depend on God, and since the Lausanne Covenant (1974) have affirmed social concern for the poor as part of Christian duty alongside evangelism, without making poverty a condition of salvation.

title: A Prophet Who Visits and Forgives
sum: In Capernaum a centurion, a Gentile friend of the Jewish community, sends elders and then friends to ask Jesus to heal his dying slave; he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof, and Jesus is amazed at his faith. At Nain Jesus meets a funeral, and moved for a widow who has lost her only son, he touches the bier and raises the young man. The crowd cries that a great prophet has arisen and God has visited his people.

John the Baptist, hearing of it in prison, sends to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One. Jesus answers with what the messengers see: Isaiah's signs of the age to come. He then praises John as more than a prophet, and rebukes a generation that rejected both John's fasting and his own feasting. The chapter ends at a Pharisee's dinner, where a woman known as a sinner weeps on Jesus' feet, dries them with her hair and anoints them. Jesus tells his host a parable of two debtors and declares her many sins forgiven.
readings: Luke has just recalled Elijah's help for a widow of Sidon and Elisha's healing of a Syrian (4:25–27). Chapter 7 acts it out: a Gentile's servant healed, a widow's only son raised near Shunem in words from 1 Kings 17. Jesus is the prophet like Elijah, but the crowd's "great prophet" is not the whole answer.

Each scene raises the question of Jesus' identity: the centurion's faith in his word, the crowd's prophet, John's Coming One, Simon's doubt ("if he really were a prophet"), and the guests' question, "Who is this man, that he even forgives sins?" Luke lets the reader answer.

The outsiders respond and the insiders hesitate: a Gentile soldier, a widow, tax collectors and a sinful woman "prove God right," while the Pharisees and lawyers set aside God's plan. Luke does not make this a rule about groups: Jewish elders plead for the centurion, and a Pharisee invites Jesus home.

views.H: Capernaum had a garrison and a synagogue; Gentile benefactors of synagogues are known from inscriptions. Nain lay near Shunem in the Jezreel Valley. Funerals followed death within a day, with processions and hired mourners. Herod Antipas held John in prison at Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea (Josephus, Antiquities 18.116–119). Banquets were eaten reclining on couches, and courtyards could admit onlookers.
views.C: The centurion story is from the double tradition (Matthew 8:5–13; compare John 4:46–54), with Luke's two delegations unique. Nain (7:11–17) and the woman at the Pharisee's house (7:36–50) are Luke's own material, though the anointing story has relatives in Mark 14:3–9 and John 12:1–8. John's question and Jesus' words about John (7:18–35) closely match Matthew 11:2–19. Luke's ordering places the raising of the dead just before Jesus says "the dead are raised."
views.L: Luke arranges the chapter so that Jesus' answer to John (7:22) summarizes what the reader has just seen: healing (7:1–10), the dead raised (7:11–17), the poor given good news (6:20). The parable of children in the market (7:31–35) is answered at once by the dinner: the woman weeps where "this generation" would not. The narrator calls Jesus "the Lord" for the first time (7:13).
views.J: The centurion is presented as a Gentile who loves Israel, much like the God-fearers of Acts, and Jewish elders vouch for him. The raising at Nain is told in the words of Israel's Scriptures. The meal with Simon belongs to Luke's pattern of Jesus dining with Pharisees (11:37; 14:1); Simon is a polite host learning a lesson, not a villain. Amy-Jill Levine warns against reading Simon's lapse in hospitality as a portrait of Jewish coldness.
views.T: The centurion's words became the Mass's prayer before Communion: "Lord, I am not worthy." The woman of 7:36–50 was merged in the West with Mary Magdalene and became the model of the penitent, painted weeping with her jar of ointment; the Eastern church kept them apart and sings of the sinful woman in the hymn of Kassiani in Holy Week. The widow of Nain's son became a symbol of the church as a mother whose children are raised.

deep.h: One anointing or several? The sinful woman and Mary Magdalene
deep.b:
Four Gospel stories tell of a woman anointing Jesus: Mark 14:3–9 and Matthew 26:6–13 (an unnamed woman pours oil on his head in Bethany, in Simon the leper's house, before the Passover); John 12:1–8 (Mary of Bethany anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair, six days before the Passover); and Luke 7:36–50 (a sinful woman, in Galilee, at Simon the Pharisee's house, anoints his feet). Some scholars think there was one event told in several ways; others think Luke's story is a separate event whose details later mixed with the Bethany story in the tradition John used. Luke himself tells no anointing at Bethany.

Luke introduces Mary Magdalene in the very next verses (8:2) as a woman freed from seven demons, with no hint that she is the woman of chapter 7. In a homily of AD 591 (Homily 33), Pope Gregory the Great identified the sinful woman, Mary of Bethany and Mary Magdalene as one person, and the seven demons with seven vices. Western art and devotion followed for a thousand years, making Magdalene the repentant prostitute. The Eastern churches never accepted the identification. In 1969 the revised Roman calendar separated the figures, and in 2016 her memorial was raised to a feast as "apostle to the apostles." Most scholars today, Catholic and Protestant, hold that the Gospels give no grounds for the identification.

John had promised one stronger than himself who would baptize with Spirit and fire and clear the threshing floor (3:16–17). From prison he hears of healings and meals with sinners. His question, "Are you the Coming One?", is the honest question of a prophet whose expectations are being reshaped. Jesus answers with Isaiah (35:5–6; 26:19; 61:1), the same passages he read in Nazareth (4:18–19), and a beatitude for those who are not tripped up by him. A Qumran text (4Q521) links similar signs with God's Messiah. Jesus then praises John without reserve: more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1, the greatest of those born of women. Yet the least in the kingdom is greater, because John stands at the turning of the ages (16:16). The chapter's last scene shows what the new age looks like: a sinner forgiven at a Pharisee's table.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the woman answers the children's song
deep.b: This is Claude's reading. In 7:32 Jesus compares "this generation" to children who complain, "We wailed a funeral song, but you would not weep." In the very next scene a woman weeps (7:38), while the host offers no water, no kiss, no oil. Luke uses the same verb, klaiō, for both. The woman is one of wisdom's children (7:35) who respond to God's call with tears and love, and Simon stands for those who neither wept with John nor rejoiced with Jesus. Commentators commonly note that 7:29–35 introduces 7:36–50 (tax collectors and sinners respond, Pharisees do not); the specific link between the children's lament and the woman's tears is Claude's.

echoes: Matthew 8:5–13; John 4:46–54; Acts 10:1–48; 1 Kings 17:10; 1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:8–37; Deuteronomy 18:15; 1:68; 19:44; Matthew 11:2–19; Isaiah 35:5–6; Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 61:1; 4:18–19; Malachi 3:1; Exodus 23:20; Deuteronomy 21:20; Proverbs 9:1–6; Mark 14:3–9; Matthew 26:6–13; John 12:1–8; Genesis 18:4; Psalm 23:5; 5:20–21

settings.by: A Gentile centurion in Capernaum, through Jewish elders and then friends
settings.to: Jesus, approaching the centurion's house
settings.when: When the centurion's valued slave is near death. In Matthew 8:5–13 the centurion comes to Jesus in person, with no elders or friends sent ahead.
settings.why: The elders plead the centurion's merit as a patron of the synagogue; the centurion himself sets it aside, saying he is not worthy to receive Jesus or even to come to him, and asks only for a word. His soldier's picture of authority expresses trust that Jesus' word works at a distance.
settings.readers: Luke's Gentile readers saw in the centurion a forerunner of Cornelius and of themselves: Gentiles who honor Israel and trust Jesus without claiming any right to him.

settings.to: The crowd following him
settings.when: On hearing the centurion's message
settings.why: To hold up a Gentile's trust as greater than any he has met in Israel, preparing Jesus' Jewish followers for the faith of the nations.

settings.by: The crowd of disciples, townspeople and mourners
settings.to: God, and one another
settings.when: When the widow's son sits up and speaks
settings.why: In awe they give glory to God and name what they have seen: a great prophet raised up, and God visiting his people as Zechariah had sung (1:68).
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the acclamation was true but incomplete: Jesus is a prophet, and more.

settings.by: John the Baptist, through two disciples; Jesus' reply
settings.to: Jesus; then John, through the messengers
settings.when: While John is imprisoned by Herod Antipas (3:20), after reports of Jesus' miracles reach him. Matthew 11:2 says John heard in prison of "the Messiah's works"; Luke has John's disciples report "all these events," just after the raising at Nain.
settings.why: John asks whether Jesus is the one he announced. Jesus answers by letting the messengers witness healings and by pointing to Isaiah's signs of God's new age, then adds a blessing on anyone not put off by the kind of Messiah he is.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, some perhaps from circles that honored John (Acts 18:25; 19:1–7), learned how John's mission and Jesus' fit together.
views: Most modern readers take the question as real doubt or perplexity.
Many church fathers held that John knew the answer and sent his disciples to be convinced.

settings.what: Jesus' words about John and "this generation"
settings.to: The crowds, after John's messengers leave
settings.when: Following the exchange with John's disciples
settings.why: To vindicate John as more than a prophet and Malachi's messenger, to place him at the threshold of the kingdom, and to expose a generation that rejected both John's austerity and Jesus' joyful meals. The narrator's aside (7:29–30) shows who accepted God's plan and who refused it.
settings.readers: Luke's readers were shown that the rejection of Jesus by some leaders was not new: it had begun with John.

settings.what: The parable of the children in the market
settings.to: The crowds; aimed at "the people of this generation"
settings.when: As the climax of his words about John
settings.why: To picture the hearers as children who will join no game, neither the dirge of John nor the dance of Jesus, and so reject God's wisdom in both. Matthew 11:16–19 has the same parable in the same setting.

settings.what: The parable of the two debtors and the woman forgiven
settings.to: Simon the Pharisee, his host, with the other guests listening; then the woman
settings.when: At dinner, after the woman anoints Jesus' feet and Simon silently judges both
settings.why: To lead Simon to judge rightly, to show that great love answers great forgiveness, and to declare publicly to the woman that her sins are forgiven and her faith has saved her. The other guests are left asking who Jesus is.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, in churches that included people with shameful pasts, learned how forgiven sinners were to be welcomed, and how the respectable could miss what God was doing.
views: Most read the parable as showing her love was the fruit of forgiveness already received.
Some, especially older Catholic interpreters, read 7:47 as forgiveness granted because of her loving contrition.

traditions.q: "Her sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much": does love earn forgiveness, or show it?
views: Catholic teaching holds that perfect contrition, sorrow "arising from a love by which God is loved above all else," obtains forgiveness even before sacramental confession, provided it includes the intention to confess (Catechism 1452; Trent, session 14). Older Catholic exegesis often saw the woman's love as such contrition; many modern Catholic scholars (Fitzmyer) read her love as the sign of forgiveness received, in line with the parable.

The Apology of the Augsburg Confession (article 4) answers opponents who cited this verse for merit: Christ himself explains it in 7:50, "Your faith has saved you." Her love shows her faith; it is faith that receives forgiveness.

Calvin argued that "for" here marks evidence, not cause: the parable shows that love follows forgiveness, so her love was proof that she had already been forgiven, and he rejected using the verse to support merit.

The Orthodox Church reads the story as repentance, love and divine mercy working together, without setting faith and love against each other. In Holy Week it sings the hymn of Kassiani, in which the sinful woman, "perceiving your divinity," brings myrrh and tears and asks for mercy.

title: Hearing the Word, and Who Hears It
sum: Jesus travels from town to town with the Twelve and a group of women he has healed, among them Mary Magdalene and Joanna, the wife of Herod's steward, who support the mission from their own means. To a great crowd he tells the parable of the sower, explains to his disciples that the seed is the word of God, and teaches about hearing well: a lamp set on its stand, nothing hidden that will not come out, and a warning to watch how you listen. When his mother and brothers come, he names as his family those who hear the word of God and do it.

Then come four acts of power. He calms a storm on the lake. On the Gentile shore he frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, who go into a herd of pigs that rushes into the lake; the healed man is sent home to tell what God has done. Back across the lake, a synagogue leader named Jairus begs him to come to his dying daughter. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his tassel and is healed, and Jesus calls her daughter. News comes that the girl has died; Jesus says "Just believe," takes her hand, and her spirit returns.
readings: Read as a chapter about hearing

Luke binds the chapter with the word "hear": the four soils are four hearers, the lamp and the measure teach how to listen, and Jesus' family are those who hear and do. The miracles that follow test the disciples' hearing: in the storm they have heard and still fear.
Read as a series of rescues

The storm, the demons, the illness and death are four kinds of chaos. In each Jesus speaks or touches, and life is restored: the sea calmed, the man clothed and in his mind, the woman made whole, the girl raised. The word "saved" runs through them (8:36, 48, 50).

The storm recalls the Psalms in which only the LORD stills the sea, and Jonah asleep in the ship. The man among the tombs with the pigs recalls Isaiah 65:4. The girl's spirit returning recalls Elijah's prayer for the widow's son (1 Kings 17:21–22).

views.H: Women traveling with a teacher and paying his costs was unusual but not unknown; Joanna's husband served at Antipas' court in Tiberias. The lake's sudden storms come down from the surrounding heights. The eastern shore was Gentile country tied to the Decapolis cities, where pigs were raised. A first-century boat found at Ginosar in 1986 shows the size of the disciples' boat.
views.C: After his own material in 7:1–8:3, Luke returns to Mark (Mark 4:1–25; 3:31–35; 4:35–5:43) and follows it closely but shortens it: he omits the seed growing secretly and the mustard seed (which he has at 13:18–19), moves the true family scene after the parables, drops Aramaic words and some vivid details, and softens the disciples' faults. His explanation of the sower uses the church's vocabulary (believe and be saved, the word of God, endurance).
views.L: Luke frames 8:4–21 with the theme of hearing and 8:22–56 with four miracles of increasing difficulty: nature, demons, disease and death. The women of 8:1–3 introduce characters who will be at the cross and the tomb (23:49, 55; 24:10). The woman and Jairus' daughter are interwoven by the number twelve and the word "daughter." The Gerasene man sent home as a witness anticipates the Gentile mission of Acts.
views.J: Every scene touches Jewish law and custom: women's place in public life, the tassels of Numbers 15, the impurity of a flow of blood (Leviticus 15), tombs and pigs as unclean, a synagogue leader as a respected figure. Amy-Jill Levine and Paula Fredriksen warn against sermons that make the woman an outcast banned by Jewish law; nothing forbade her to be in the crowd or to touch Jesus. Jairus, a synagogue leader, comes to Jesus in faith.
views.T: Mary Magdalene, honored in the East as "equal to the apostles," was merged in the West with the sinful woman of chapter 7 until the 20th century. The sower was a favorite text for preaching on the hearing of the Word, and "those who hear the word of God and do it" for teaching about Mary as model disciple. Healing services and prayers for the sick often read the woman with the flow of blood and Jairus' daughter together.

deep.b:
Luke 8:1–3 is the only passage in the Gospels that names women traveling with Jesus during his Galilean ministry, and it says they paid for the mission. Mark and Matthew mention such women only at the cross (Mark 15:40–41; Matthew 27:55–56). Luke names three: Mary Magdalene, freed from seven demons; Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza, a woman of the court; and Susanna, otherwise unknown. Two of them, Mary Magdalene and Joanna, reappear as the first witnesses of the empty tomb (24:10).

Scholars read the passage in different ways. Some see Luke as unusually positive about women, giving them places as disciples and patrons (Witherington, Bauckham). Others argue that Luke praises women chiefly in supporting roles, silent and serving, while men preach (Barbara Reid, Turid Karlsen Seim discuss this "double message"). Both agree that the presence of named women in Jesus' company is historically remarkable. How the passage bears on women's leadership in the church today is argued on the topic page for women in church leadership.

Luke follows Mark's order of sower, explanation, lamp, storm, demoniac and the two daughters, but his changes show his concerns. He moves Jesus' family from before the parables (Mark 3:31–35) to after them, so they become an example of hearing. He has Jesus speak to crowds from town after town, not from a boat. He uses "lake" instead of "sea," "Master" instead of "Teacher," and softens the disciples' rebuke in the storm. In the Gerasene story he adds "the Abyss" and that the man was "saved." In the woman's story he does not say the doctors made her worse (compare Mark 5:26), a change some have linked to the tradition that Luke was a physician. He drops Mark's Aramaic "Talitha koum." Henry Cadbury showed that many such changes improve Mark's Greek style.

settings.to: A great crowd gathering from town after town
settings.when: During his tour of Galilee with the Twelve and the women. Mark 4:1 and Matthew 13:1–2 have Jesus teach from a boat by the sea; Luke has crowds coming from one town after another, with no boat.
settings.why: To show what happens when God's word is heard: much is lost, but where it takes root the harvest is great. The loud call to hear makes the crowd ask which kind of ground they are.
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew believers who had fallen away under pressure or been choked by wealth and cares. The parable explained it and urged them to hold on.
views: Many scholars (Jeremias, Dodd) think the parable first promised a great harvest despite losses.
Luke's explanation stresses the hearers' response and endurance.

settings.to: His disciples, who ask what the parable means
settings.when: After the parable of the sower
settings.why: To tell those who ask that they have received the gift of knowing God's mysteries, while for others the parables remain riddles, in the pattern of Isaiah's mission. Luke keeps only a brief echo of Isaiah 6 and saves the full text for the end of Acts.
settings.readers: Luke's readers understood why many did not believe, and that insight is a gift, not a reward.

settings.to: His disciples
settings.when: In answer to their question
settings.why: To identify the seed as the word of God and the soils as kinds of hearers: those robbed by the devil, those who fall away in testing, those choked by cares, wealth and pleasures, and those who hold the word fast and bear fruit by endurance.
settings.readers: Luke's wording speaks directly to the church: believing and being saved, falling away in testing, enduring.

settings.what: The lamp and the measure of hearing
settings.to: His disciples, with the crowd near
settings.when: Following the explanation of the sower. Matthew 5:15 uses the lamp saying in the Sermon on the Mount, of the disciples as light; Luke, like Mark 4:21–25, puts it after the sower, of what is hidden coming into the open.
settings.why: To promise that what is now hidden in parables will come into the open, and to warn hearers that how they listen decides whether they gain more or lose what they seem to have.

settings.to: The people who bring him word that his mother and brothers are outside
settings.when: When his family cannot reach him for the crowd. Mark 3:20–21, 31–35 places this before the parables, after his family has set out to take hold of him; Luke places it after them, without that hint of conflict.
settings.why: To name as his mother and brothers all who hear the word of God and do it. In Luke the saying widens his family rather than rejecting his relatives; Mary herself has been the model hearer (1:38).
settings.readers: Gentile readers learned that they belonged to Jesus' family through hearing and obeying, not through birth.

settings.to: The disciples in the boat
settings.when: Crossing the lake, when a sudden gale threatens to sink them
settings.why: The disciples cry for rescue; Jesus silences wind and water and asks where their faith is. The scene leaves them, and the reader, asking who commands the sea as only God does.
settings.readers: For churches buffeted by persecution, the boat in the storm became a picture of the church kept safe by its Lord.

settings.by: The possessed man (the demons speaking through him), Jesus, and later the man himself
settings.to: Jesus; then the man's own town
settings.when: On the Gentile shore, as Jesus steps out of the boat
settings.why: The demons plead not to be sent to the Abyss; Jesus frees the man, who then asks to follow. Jesus instead sends him home to tell what God has done, making him the first witness among Gentiles. The townspeople, afraid, ask Jesus to leave.
settings.readers: Luke's Gentile readers saw a Gentile delivered and sent as a witness, a first sign of the mission in Acts.
views: Most read the story as a deliverance showing Jesus' power over demons.
Some scholars hear protest against Roman occupation in the name "Legion" and the pigs rushing into the sea.

settings.what: Jairus' daughter and the woman with the flow of blood
settings.by: Jairus, the woman, Jesus, and a messenger from Jairus' house
settings.to: Jesus; the crowd; Jairus and his wife
settings.when: On Jesus' return across the lake, as the crowd presses around him
settings.why: Jairus pleads for his dying only daughter; on the way a woman is healed by touching Jesus' tassel and is called into the open to tell her story and hear herself called "daughter." When the girl dies, Jesus tells Jairus, "Just believe," raises her with a word and a touch, and orders silence.
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned that faith reaches Jesus even when others despair, and that Jesus' power over death is a sign of the resurrection to come.
